extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for reasoning about numbers, algebra, geometry, and — chiefly — the grounds on which we should disbelieve asserted facts (distinguishing improbability, impossibility, and the strength of inductive laws). Includes criteria for when mathematical methods apply to physical inquiry and how to judge extraordinary claims (e.g., miracles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of formation defines number
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a number connotes the manner in which single objects of the given kind must be put together to produce that aggregate (e.g., two pebbles means one pebble joined to one pebble; three may be 1+1+1 or 1+(2), etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every arithmetical proposition is a statement of one of the modes of formation of a given number; statements about operations (e.g., cube of 12 = 1728) assert particular modes of composing aggregates and their reversibility (e.g., cube root decomposition). Modes of formation can be combined or reduced deductively to determine other modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a uniform mode of formation in numerical nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is advantageous to select a mode of formation which shall be alike for all numbers, fixing the connotation of names of number on one uniform principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A uniform principle aids retention and comprehension; our numeral system conveys two modes of formation for every number (succession by unit and composition by powers of ten), which is pedagogically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sums of equals are equals (fundamental inductive law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comprehensive law 'The sums of equals are equals' (and the related truth that whatever is made up of parts is made up of the parts of those parts) is the inductive law that renders arithmetic deductive and is the warrant for calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical conclusions (e.g., 5 + 2 = 7) rest on this inductive law combined with definitions; arithmetic operations are applications of this law or of laws deducible from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of functions and use of algebraic notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions classify modes of formation of numbers (e.g., x+a, ax, log_a x, sin x). Algebraic notation (a, b, n, (a+b)^n, etc.) expresses relationships without specifying particular numbers, enabling general reasonings about functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general problem of algebraical calculus is: given a function F of a number, find F as applied to any function of that number (e.g., binomial theorem shows how (a+b)^n is a function of a and b). Simple functions can be composed to form more complex functions; algebraic notation is required for such generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry's premises: a few axioms and explicit definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry rests on a few general axioms (including 'the sums of equals are equals', 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another', and that magnitudes which can be made to coincide are equal) plus definitions asserting the existence of geometrical objects (straight lines, circles, angles, parallels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These minimal premises enable deduction of many theorems because geometry reduces position and figure to questions of magnitude and relies on general laws connecting magnitudes, lines, angles, and enclosed spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as the exemplar of the deductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical training is the most perfect type of the deductive method; its processes teach philosophers to apply laws of simpler phenomena to explain and predict more complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value of mathematical instruction is mainly methodological: learning how to employ laws of simpler systems to reason about more complex systems, not merely the content of mathematical doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of applicability of mathematical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical principles are manifestly inapplicable where (1) causes are imperfectly accessible to observation, (2) causes are numerous and intermixed so that computation of aggregate effect exceeds the calculus, or (3) causes are in perpetual fluctuation (e.g., chemistry, physiology, social science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical accuracy is often obtained at the expense of reality; beyond astronomy and closely analogous phenomena, mathematical solutions become progressively more difficult and imperfect. Use mathematics when numerical laws can be ascertained and aggregate computations are tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disbelief (distinct from mere absence of belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbelief is not mere lack of belief; it is being fully persuaded that some opinion is not true so that, even if apparently strong evidence were produced, we would believe the witnesses false or mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds for abstaining from belief (suspension) differ from grounds for active disbelief; the chapter focuses on when and why we are entitled to disbelieve asserted facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive evidence in extraordinary claims is always approximate
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive evidence produced in support of assertions which are nevertheless rejected on the score of impossibility or improbability is never full proof but is grounded on some approximate generalization (e.g., testimony, perception may be imperfect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since affirmative evidence is typically approximate, assessment depends on comparing the strength/order of approximate generalizations supporting both affirmative and negative sides; stronger generalizations warrant disbelief of the weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with a complete induction: impossibility and total disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alleged fact contradicts a completed generalization grounded on rigorous induction (a law of nature), it is said to be impossible and is to be disbelieved totally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law established by sufficient experiment and observation excludes credible counter-instances absent adequate counteracting causes; to accept the contrary would require evidence equivalent to that on which the law was founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of evidence required to overthrow a law established by experimentum crucis
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a cause–effect law has been established by decisive experiments (experimentsum crucis) and repeated observations so as to exclude error, any assertion that the effect did not follow when the cause occurred (without counteracting cause) must be disbelieved unless evidence is provided that would suffice to overturn the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reject such a law requires evidence of the same high order as that on which the law was accepted; otherwise we should prefer the law over any amount of approximate affirmative testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle assessment: new cause vs contradiction of law
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction to the law of cause and effect but is alleged to be a new effect produced by the introduction of a new cause (a direct interposition of a willful being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a miracle is credible depends on prior belief in such a being and on comparing the hypotheses 'supernatural agency' versus 'unknown natural cause'; unknown natural causes cannot be completely ruled out, so miracles require extraordinary antecedent probability to outweigh the presumption of uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare approximate generalizations to judge improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the approximate generalizations leading to the affirmative are collectively weaker (further from universality) than those which support the negative, the proposition is improbable and should be provisionally disbelieved; otherwise belief may be warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment is made by weighing the preponderance of approximate generalizations; provisional disbelief follows when negative-side generalizations are stronger until further sifting of evidence occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbelief requires absence of adequate counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To assert that a cause existed without its usual effect is only a ground for disbelief when that absence occurred in the absence of any adequate counteracting cause; if a counteracting cause could plausibly have been present, disbelief is not mandated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment involves estimating the probability that known or unknown counteracting causes were present at the specific time and place, using knowledge of their frequency/rarity and other marks they would likely leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical method for assessing unknown causes' plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not asked to pronounce on the general probability of unknown causes in nature, but only on their having existed at the particular time and place alleged; one may often judge this from whether their presence would have manifested other marks or been observed elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the known frequency/rarity and expected concomitant signs of such causes to estimate the antecedent improbability of their presence in the specific case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conflicts with causal laws from conflicts with properties of kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: A more common form of conflict is not with causal laws but with uniformities of mere co-existence (properties of Kinds) — e.g., travelers' marvels about people with tails, wings, or others — which are cases of improbability relative to known properties of kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such reports skeptically until confirmed by experience; evaluate against existing uniformities of co-existence and seek corroborating observation before acceptance.
